**Abstract**: Network scholarship regularly leverages visualizations. 
They are thought to enhance readers' recall, interpretation, and simplification of scholar's intended takeaways. 
However, by representing the specifics of single empirical cases, these visualization strategies may not optimize how well they accomplish our scientific purposes. 
I describe how visualizations often target three non-overlapping sets of aims simultaneously--exploratory description, theoretical conceptualization, *and* empirical interpretation bridging between those. 
I then highlight how these orientations both necessitate constrain different sets of the varied scientific purposes and principles of visualization. 
Given these differential demands, this paper provokes the field to consider whether presenting *modeled* network results--in lieu of empirical cases--better satisfies the aims of visualization for particular purposes.

\textcolor{red}{NOTE: In preparation for submission to the \textit{Social Networks} theory special issue (which has a submission timeline of Nov 1.)}

\newpage

Social network research relies heavily on data visualization [@freeman2004]. 
These visualizations can serve to characterize, simplify, and focus empirical and/or theoretical claims [@moody2005; @rawlings2023]. 
Visualizations are generally more readily digestible than tables of (seemingly endless) coefficients, significance tests, and summary statistics [@healy2018; @schwabish2021]. 
Additionally, with the increasing ubiquity of network verbiage in society, they can even convey ideas in ways that require less "translation" work for audiences from outside of academic and research niches [@sayama2016; @wolff2026]. 
Quite simply, network visualization is not only common, but can be incredibly useful [@birkett2021].^[As with any data presentation strategy--visual or otherwise--there are also ample examples of how to do this poorly (e.g., what have come to be known as unintelligible network "hairballs"); I have a few published visuals of my own that I'd *substantially* rework if given the opportunity today.]

Traditionally, this has taken the form of directly visualizing instances(s) of empirically **observed** social networks--whether snapshots of single data waves, or evolving network "movies" for dynamic relational data patterns [@ognyanova2025].^[These typically occur *after* data pre-processing has taken place (e.g., cleaning, recoding, etc.), but no further data reduction steps (i.e., are not the product of data *summaries* or analytic interpretations).]
That is, such visualizations are intended to characterize the data *per se*. 
While this practice predominates, it's worth asking: 
(1) what are purposes that motivate why we visualize, and 
(2) what additional requirements govern appropriate strategies for accomplishing those aims, then 
(3) whether (there are conditions for which) an alternative strategy serves those *purposes* and *principles* better than the existing approach?

In this paper, my answers to this set of questions suggests many practices of social network visualization are currently misaligned to their purposes--or more precisely, assumes a *single* visualization orientation can successfully address *multiple* sets of aims. 
As is often the case with split allegiances [@pache2010], I contend our current approach could be adjusted to better convey (especially the) *theoretical* takeaways of social networks research.
In particular, I contend that an occasional misalignment between these aims, many--but definitely not all--uses of social network visualizations would be better served by visualizing "modeled" networks rather than "observed" network data. 
I also address how the corollary principles of best practices apply across these differentiated visualization strategies.
After making this case following the motivations above, I illustrate this shift in three ways--a trivial example common to how many of us already teach social network modeling, describing several existing strategies that leverage similar properties, and an applied example from a recent research paper.

Before continuing, I should emphasize that when I say "model" I intend this usage in a *theoretical*, not a *statistical* sense. 
I avoid relegating this point to a footnote to highlight that the strategy I encourage does not apply only to statistically modeled results. 
Moreover, I should emphasize that this broader applicability in some ways reflects that my proposal in places *imports* practices from non-statistical orientations to network research as much as (or perhaps even more so) than developing a method for statistical applications that can be exported to other use cases.
That caveat noted, my illustrations below will primarily draw on statistical applications as a concrete demonstration; but I will include how the approach apples beyond these particularities.^[Specifically, some of the elements proposed below are directly adopted from other corners of SNA where they are already variably common practices (if labeled differently), and (partially) pave the way for how statistically oriented researchers can implement the approach.]

## Why (network) visualization?
So, what are the benefits of network data visualizations? 
And what are the principles we should follow to best achieve those benefits? 
Here, I begin from the assumption that SNA visualizations seek to optimize their *scientific utility* (broadly construed), and highlight some shortcomings that have emerged in our common practices, which have weakened our ability to accomplish those aims--particularly by assuming a single visualization strategy can address multiple (sometimes competing) sets of aims.

Many of the benefits for network scholarship mirror those that motivate data visualization in science more broadly, especially regarding communication clarity [@rawlings2023]. 
A fundamental premise is that data visualization enhances **memory** [@schwabish2021]; this reflects what we know from a number of old adages--including that there's simply value in beauty [@tufte2006; @halpern2015]. 
Moreover, this memory benefit leverages the potential **efficiency** available in data visualization that simply cannot be achieved in other strategies for presenting evidence [@healy2018].^[There are many pithy statements about the vast amounts of information that can be conveyed in a single image.]
Edward Tufte has prioritized not only using this benefit, but attempting to find ways to optimize it, e.g., via efforts to maximize what he called the "ink-to-information" ratio [@tufte1983].
These memory-oriented enhancements can arise both via improved encoding processes *and* recall--e.g., the simple act of including visualizations leverages the complementary of multi-modal communication strategies' differential strengths and weaknesses (e.g., compared to text) [@sweller1988].

The data we use to represent social processes are almost always inherently high-dimensional, and visualizations provide a means for **simplifying** that complexity in structured, interpretable formats [@wickham2023a].^[Some contend that this is a *constraint* of data visualization imposed on data presentation strategies (by obfuscating its richness), rather than its benefit [@healy2014].]
This leads visualizations to not only enhance communicative aims, but also to improve readers' ability to understand and interpret complex social phenomenon [@schwabish2021]. 
While statistics can summarize data in principled ways, data visualization rarely simply mimics these other forms and representations of data reduction. 
Instead, they are also "attention-drawing" efforts that highlight certain features of the data, while simultaneously deprioritizing others [@leifer1992].

So, how do network scholars *in particular* prioritize these combating aims?
Network scholars especially leverage these dimension reduction approaches by translating summaries of (theoretically) salient *social space* into the approaches for producing visualized representations [@rawlings2023]. 
For example, one such "attention-drawing" move a research may use would highlight certain relational patterns (e.g., community structure), while deprioritizing others (e.g., homophily).^[For example, to emphasize the changes in political polarization over time in the US Congress, @moody2013 employ increased coarse-graining to highlight *group* size and positioning over time, and juxtapose that against the decreased *individual* positioning and distancing.]

While such trade-offs may seem generally useful, I argue that how researchers prioritize among these various aims frequently (even if implicitly) differ across different stages of the research process, each of which may leverage visualization as a tool. 
Given these differentiated aims across research stages, applying a single "typical" approach to network visualization may limit the utility of *visualizations* for the particularized purposes at different stages.
That is, my hope is the encourage, more, more-varied, and more tailored uses of visualizations in ways that will afford each instance a greater likelihood of achieving the researchers' needs.
In particular, optimal visualization strategies differ substantially between exploratory [@wickham2023a], conceptual/theoretical [@brady2020], or explanatory aims [@healy2014]. 

## Multidimensional aims: scientific purposes and principles, across research stages

Yet realizing these common aims in practice requires navigating competing demands arising from multiple dimensions of research.
First, I distinguish several distinct scientific **purposes**---the communicative reasons for employing visualization. 
Second, I identify additional scientific **principles** that govern visualization practices in pursuing those purposes.
Third, I differentiate three **stages** of research in which visualizations can prove useful: exploration, conceptualization, and explanation.
Together, these dimensions show how particular visualization practices necessarily prioritize different **combinations** of these purposes and principles as their roles shift across the stages of the research process.

### Scientific **purposes** of network visualization
A first dimension in leveraging the utility of network visualizations concerns the various purposes they may accomplish.
Although these purposes principally orient visualization toward distinct goals, they are not fully mutually exclusive [@healy2014].

*Description* seeks to systematically characterize patterns, such as general tendencies or variation, to capture the state of things as they are as accurately as possible [@schwabish2021].
In networks, this can span multiple levels—including features of nodes, ties, sections within networks, or networks as a whole [@rawlings2023; @moody2005].

*Case interpretation* makes sense of the particularities of a case, which can help identify its important features as contrasted against the alternatives that could have been [@ragin1992; @collins2024].
Additionally, this provides a lens through which to assess how broadly those observed features should inform our understanding of the wider social setting the case represents [@ayala2019].

*Simplification* reduces complexity to focus and attune attention to particular features of a social process, while necessarily de-prioritizing other elements [@healy2018; @leifer1992].
This process often involves decisions about classificatory boundaries and labeling those distinctions [@wickham2023a; @healy2014].

Researchers’ *theoretical interpretations* bring empirical observations and broader theoretical frameworks to bear on one another, establishing “what is this a case of?” [@ragin1992].
In this use, visualizations help identify what we have learned through the lens of theoretical expectations, including what our data reinforce, fail to support, or suggest requires further refinement [@borgatti2011a; @liu2017].

### Scientific **principles** for visualization practice
Before turning to how visualizations can optimize these purposes across particular tasks, I describe two additional scientific principles that govern how researchers pursue these ends, which should guide any (network) data visualization.

Network visualizations often present unique *ethical* challenges, particularly concerning potential *confidentiality* and *deductive disclosure* [@adams2019a; @ortizruiz2026].
The potential for deductive disclosure is broad in any presentation of multiple variables [@rocher2019], especially in the “closed population” settings common in network research [but see also @zimmer2010].
Relational data provide additional avenues for serial deductive disclosure [@narayanan2009].^[I.e., the revealed identity of one node in a graph (e.g., myself) can in turn heighten the capacity to identify others (e.g., my friends).]
To this end, the frequent practice of plotting empirical networks from data collection efforts may undermine principles of confidentiality and minimal risk, which should lead us to consider alternative visualization strategies that can leverage visualization’s strengths while minimizing those potential risks [@ortizruiz2026].
These limitations do not preclude network researchers from visualizing, and even sharing, data [@pasquale2025].
Rather, they suggest that we need to tailor our approaches in ways that current practices do not necessarily optimize.

While the benefits of open-science principles are not new [@partha1994], researchers have recently (re-)discovered enthusiasm for better implementation in practice [@miguel2019].^[In fact, in personal communication, one colleague noted that the “sociogram is … one of the purest original forms of open science, [… and] replicable data transparency.”]
*Replicability* therefore raises particularly thorny questions for (network) visualizations.^[While the existing literature sometimes uses "replicable" and "reproducible" interchangeably, and others distinguishing them, those distinctions have at times been employed in exactly opposite ways [@miguel2019]. For clarity, I use only *replicability* to indicate the ability to recreate a visualization in the same way as the original, whether data-linked or otherwise.]
Network visualizations entail a combination of node/tie inclusion and exclusion rules, their respective attribute information, and determinations of the positioning of each.^[Given the aims of this paper, I focus on the replication of *network visualizations* independently of the numerous additional appropriate considerations for how to implement replicable and reproducible research more broadly [@miguel2019], including the particular demands of network research [@neal2024b; @pasquale2025].]
This forces consideration of what scope of information (i.e., which variables for which nodes and which ties) and granularity of presentation (e.g., levels of measurement per observation) we include in visualizations.
In particular, visualization’s utility may not require including this information in the full detail available in the data.
Additionally, because positions in network visualizations are typically defined relatively (vs. absolutely), algorithmic and procedural details (e.g., random-number-generator seeds) can be important for faithfully recreating visualizations that are substantively or aesthetically comparable [@bender-demoll2005].

### Network visualization across research **stages**

While research processes entail many potential stages, three commonly employ visualizations as a primary tool.
I therefore next outline a stylized typology of visualization strategies that roughly correspond with different stages of research, and consider how they differentially prioritize the purposes and accommodate the principles described above.
To foreshadow, this differentiation leads to a suggested strategy of visualizing *modeled analytic results* as a unique combination that remains under-used in network research—a practice I outline in the following section.

*Observed* network visualizations provide a means for examining the case(s) at hand.
These characterizations help researchers become familiar with the nature of their data [@martin2018], both by describing general node, tie, or network patterns of composition and structure and by identifying potential needs for analysis [@freeman2000].^[For example, this entails the pre-processing steps of variable reclassification or anomalous-case handling, [@wickham2023a].]
This stage often prioritizes fidelity to exploring the features in the data, accounting for what they contain [@bender-demoll2005].

A primary approach to visualizing network data prioritizes this purpose, shaping researchers’ understanding of patterns in the data and--when included in publications--attempting to do the same for readers.
While this is often a “first step” toward examining and presenting one’s case, it does not mean that the visualization directly “reflects” reality.
It merely indicates that the data have been obtained, minimally processed, shaped into a coherent presentation strategy, and presented to the reader [@wickham2023a; @healy2018].

The fundamental steps to generating observed network visualizations are: (1) obtaining the data (through primary methods or secondary sources), (2) pre-processing, cleaning, and organizing the data, (3) reducing to focal elements (relational and nodal attributes), (4) transforming that reduction to visual form, and (5) labeling it.
While these necessarily entail some degree of simplification--because visualizations cannot capture the data’s high dimensionality--this stage seeks to minimize simplifications or “rotate” the visualization’s priorities sufficiently to examine data's complexity by iterating through multiple simplifications, one at a time.
If included in published papers, this type of visualization serves a similar purpose to the “descriptive statistics” Table 1 that many papers provide—giving the reader a means to orient to the case at hand with a distilled summary.
However, publishing observed network visualizations can lead to visuals that are overly complex in ways that obfuscate what we can learn from them, draw attention to the particularities of the case, rather than the general principles the case is examined to characterize, be difficult to precisely replicate, raising questions about consistency in interpretation, and introduce potential risks that could violate research ethical standards.

Although primarily descriptive, this type of visualization can also bridge to the analytic aims of research, seeding potential analyses for more inductively oriented work or beginning the process of case interpretation in more deductively oriented work.
Many of the pre-processing, presentation, and sense-making steps involved at this stage benefit from intimate knowledge of the data [@potterat2004a].
Although this knowledge can inform researchers’ work, it may undermine principles of confidentiality and/or deductive disclosure in ways that may not be advisable or permitted in publishable or directly replicable forms [@ortizruiz2026].

Some fields readily draw on *conceptual models*, to varying degrees of formalization—ranging from those that primarily serve to “organize one’s thoughts” [@brady2020] to approaches that formally articulate analytic aims and assumptions [e.g., directed acyclic graphs; @elwert2013].
Network research has periodically leveraged such visualization aims to specify how *combinations* of features can lead expectations to diverge from various “ideal type” formations of networks.
Visualizations can make these configurations concrete in ways that may not be as readily intelligible without them.^[A very widely used example of this is how “small world” networks, while being very differentiated from random networks, require few shortcuts, which does not make them appear particularly statistically distinct from “caveman” graphs, but the difference is readily apparent when visualized [@watts1998b].]

This form of visualization can explicitly articulate which elements are core to subsequent analyses and which remain unexamined assumptions, thus informing which theorized social processes the analyses evaluate [@adams2020d].
Conceptual visualizations can formalize the theoretical claims a study evaluates, including the patterns that would support, disconfirm, or suggest alternate interpretations.^[Here, visualizations are performing the same clarifying and formalizing task that is accomplished when we employ "writing as thinking" [@zinsser1993].]

In their “pure” form, conceptual visualizations tend to prioritize theoretical interpretation and simplification over all else.
Additionally, given the potential for (nearly) “data-free” visualizations of this sort, ethical considerations are likely minimal.

When used as a strategy for presenting analytic results, visualizations typically seek to highlight the *theoretical* implications of *interpretation* and/or *explanation* [@rawlings2023].
For example, in social network research with explanatory (e.g., causal) aims, researchers seek to demonstrate how observations in empirical cases [@kadushin2012] combined with appropriate analytic strategies [@borgatti2024; @mccarty2019], conform to expectations in ways that support theoretically appropriate interpretations [@borgatti2011].
In this case, simplifications tend to highlight theoretical implications over data fidelity (case interpretation).
Because an emphasis on theoretical conformity often highlights general patterns or “ideal types,” it need not rely on the specifics of the data--thus allowing researchers to readily maintain confidentiality and facilitate replication [@bender-demoll2005].

Alternatively, other research may primarily draw on theory and analysis to account for events in particular cases *per se*.
In this case simplification and (case) interpretation are still more heavily emphasized than description and full data fidelity.
Confidentiality can be maintained through presenting heuristic visualizations--e.g., to elaborate "conceptual generalizability" [@collins2024]--rather than direct representations of labeled data, also fostering potential replicability.

In sum, different research stages and visualization strategies incorporate different optimizations across the purposes and principles of network visualization. 
[**Table 1**](#benies) heuristically represents a summary of these potential combinations.

### Implications for visualization practice

As illustrated in the preceding section, visualizations often need to prioritize distinct combinations of the purposes outlined above and may need to adapt in order to adhere to the accompanying visualization principles.
This potential for non-overlapping combinations can produce sub-optimal visuzliations in several distinct ways.
Perhaps most obviously, when researchers construct a visualization to serve one of these purposes (e.g., exploratory data analysis), it will not optimally serve other aims (e.g., explanatory) because the combinations necessary to achieve one task well can trade off against the ability to optimize for other purposes.

Perhaps more problematically, when researchers *assume* (or worse, *require*) that visualizations have “universal” benefits, they presuppose that the purposes of data visualization are necessarily shared across this range of uses.
One common version of this approach in SNA produces a “descriptive” plot of the observed data and then “overlays” features of the theoretical interpretation of analytic results, in hopes that readers will recognize the “important” signal amid the remaining noise in the data.
Unfortunately, this type of compromise strategy can fail to accomplish *any* of our aims well [@pache2010].
My contention is that network visualizations not infrequently commit one of these two errors.^[For example, in instances where I have wanted to convey the theoretical takeaways from @adams2013—that different types of “risk partnerships” provide different contributions to overall graph connectivity, even while their node-level differences/combinations are minimal—I have found that nearly impossible to readily convey from the (largely exploratory-oriented) visualization we included in the paper—error 1.]
Rather than simply critiquing existing practices, I propose an alternative visualization strategy that optimizes for a combination of purposes not adequately served by our most common approaches, while maintaining the visualization principles detailed above.
In particular, I propose that “modeled network visualizations” can more readily combine theoretical interpretation with empirically grounded simplification while preserving confidentiality and facilitating replicability.

## Modeled network visualizations

My fundamental proposition is simple: rather than relying on "observed" networks to present analytic results, we should develop a strategy for presenting "modeled network visualizations."
This is not a ground-breaking suggestion.
In fact, many statistical modelers—of social network and other types of data—already enact this practice, but publications do not consistently deploy this approach in ways that fully leverages its potential utility.
For example, “eye-balling” consistency of modeled results against observed network visuals—in tandem with formal statistical tests for goodness of fit—is typically taught as a helpful practice in model development and fitting processes [@krivitsky2023].^[They can be especially helpful in identifying theoretical limitations of existing models or enhancing stability of estimates.]
However, while we use these heuristic network visualizations to improve model fit, authors still often resort to presenting the observed version as their primary network visualization(s) in publications.
I have done this multiple times myself.

"Modeled network visualizations" can provide a better alternative when we seek to characterize analytic results in ways that better achieve certain combinations of the aims and principles outlined above.^[I do not also contrast these with “conceptual” visualizations in what follows, because researchers often develop those intentionally in *non-empirical* ways.]
In describing the proposed approach and  examples below, I focus on the conditions under which modeled network visualizations offer relative advantages in pursuing this unique combination.

### Effect plots - a parallel motivation
Let me draw a few parallels that illustrate how researchers leverage (parts of) the same logic underpinning this proposed approach when presenting and interpreting modeled results.
Logistic-regression coefficients (just like exponential random graph models) are notoriously hard to make substantive sense of on their own (e.g., significance and magnitude of effects are frequently conflated in results interpretations by writers and readers alike).
Interaction terms in other forms of regression are similarly difficult to interpret.
A common solution has been for researchers to: (1) gather, pre-process, and provide a descriptive summary of their data to give an overview of what the sample being analyzed represents and how key focal features are distributed in the population; (2) conduct statistical analyses to investigate the researchers’ theoretical aims, which are summarized with traditional combinations of betas, standard errors, log-likelihoods, etc. to represent the fit of those claims to empirical estimation; and then (3) transform those modeled results into “predicted probabilities” in ways that help interpret what those modeled results “look like” in their implications [@fox2006].

To “tell the story” that arises from the model results, we do not return to the raw data, provide the individual-level combination of variables for some subset of the population, and rely on those cases’ patterns to convey the implications of our research [in the rare cases that people do, they are often “synthetic” cases, not real ones, e.g., @ayala2019].
In the case above, the right panel makes apparent that "remorse" benefit in sentencing reductions applies across groups, except for black men [@zhao2024a]. 
Deciphering that result from the left panel would be next to impossible; but we also would rarely attempt to use a descriptive plot for those purposes.
To do so would not only fail to clearly tell the aggregate story we have learned in the course of theorization and analysis.^[It is additionally well known that overly granular descriptive statistics can inadvertently pose deductive disclosure risks, thus leading to "cell size" thresholds for many reporting standards [@rocher2019].]
So why, in network research, do we so often feel uniquely compelled to present the “real” pattern of relationships from our data as a means to interpret and convey our findings in visual form?

### Blockmodels, motifs, & coefficients - partial *network* parallels
It is also important to note that the basis of the general idea—if not the complete practice I am recommending—is already in use in some domains of social network research.
Perhaps the most direct corollary is how blockmodeling results tend to be presented as a representations of role profiles [@doreian2005].
The image-matrix and/or reduced-graph presentation distills the overall role structure of an analyzed graph into summary form [@borgatti2024].
A permuted adjacency matrix arranged by density blocks maps that summary onto the full data, but typically does so for the *observed* adjacency matrix rather than for a modeled representation.
Other “coarse-graining” visualization strategies for “large” networks commonly take similar parallel approaches [@newman2004a].

Another approach to leveraging visualizations to characterize analytic results in theoretically focused ways comes via *network motifs* [@schwarze2021].
Network motifs identify *repeated* structural patterns across multiple (often, but not exclusively, *personal*) sub-graphs of networks.
They present these patterns as abstracted “common forms,” rather than presenting multiple parallel observed networks and then highlighting commonalities across the repeated panels.
These aims are similar to those in blockmodels, though network motifs exclusively consider *local* configurations.
However, network motifs—and their visual style of presentation—remain more widely adopted in network science than among social network researchers to date [for an exception see @vacca2020].
Other approaches in ego-network research similarly draw on stylized representations to visualize analytic implications, rather than reverting to empirical networks to explain findings [especially when doing so would violate confidentiality; @mccarty2019].

Such configurational representations have also been employed to assist with interpreting the results of inferential statistical models of social network data by presenting visualizations of micro-patterns rather than coefficient names in results tables [e.g., in stochastic actor-based models; @snijders2026].


## Implementing modeled network visualizations

Although modeled network visualizations can take many forms,^[Recall that I use “modeled” in a theoretical and conceptually based sense, not necessarily a statistical one.] their implementation follows a similar structure across these potential forms.
This section elaborates the four common stages of this process. 
I accompany the description with an illustrative example drawn from a strategy for teaching and model building in exponential random graph models [@krivitsky2026; @lind2012].
The final section then illustrates the approach through an empirical example.

### Step 1: Characterize the data to be examined

As with the recent resurgence in attention to the importance of *descriptive* statistics before conducting and presenting any multi-variable analyses [@ayala2019; @healy2014; @wickham2023a], the first step is to provide a preliminary account of the data to be examined.
The full details of what this should entail likely depend on the scientific aims and nature of the data to be investigated (e.g., qualitative or quantitative, closed or open population, etc.), but scholars have recently suggested potentially standardizing these to include a variety of features at the node, tie, and network levels [@neal2024b].
In some—but, as with my proposal here, *not all*—cases, an observed (network) visualization can enhance this descriptive task.
That is, my proposal doesn't exclude exploratory network visualizations, instead asking us to reconsider if they're right for our purposes.

The observed network in panel A of [**Figure 2**](#fig:greys) provides a visualization of the extended example I draw on below while developing this strategy--adapted from a widely used example developed by Benjamin Lind -@lind2012.
The data the “hookup” network among characters in *Grey’s Anatomy* and will be used in estimating an expoential random graph model (ERGM) and visualize its results.

### Step 2: Conduct an analysis appropriate to the research question
The second step is to conduct whatever analyses are appropriate to the theoretical aims of the research questions and the nature of the analytic dataset.
This step reiterates a fundamental feature of the proposal here: “modeled” results come in many forms.
While the illustration here draws from *statistical* models (ERGMs, in particular), the approach could equally be applied to *any* other form of data-analytic results—ranging from similarly statistically oriented models such as SAOMs through to the primary takeaways from grounded-theoretically oriented ethnographic observations [@dominguez2014].

Building (statistical) models of observed network data can be a complicated process.
In developing “well-behaving” models, estimating of goodness of fit can assist with interpreting what the latest model estimates are—and are not—accounting for in the data.
Many tutorials for developing such models employ visualizations of a single network instance from intermediate model results, both as a means to intuit how models work when teaching--a necessary step when enhancing model estimation and fit in real analyses [@krivitsky2026].

Examining the observed network above in light of theoretical goals,^[In empirical work, this combination likely drives both the data we collect in the first place and the elements we draw from it in exploratory/observed network visualizations.] suggests a variety of model parameters to investigate.
For example, we could fit models that include degree effects; race, gender, or age effects (both as “activity” and “homophily” parameters); or structural features (e.g., local closure rules [@adams2015]).^[In [**Figure 2**](#fig:greys) Panel A, “isolates” are not present because they were excluded by definition in the way the data were encoded, so a restriction against isolation should be part of the model.]

### Step 3: Compile an appropriate summary of analytic results

Analytic results and interpretations are necessarily reductions of the full details available in our data [@adams2020d].
Done well, they draw our attention to the scientifically useful features of the data, lead us to appropriate interpretations, and limit the distractions that keep us from achieving those aims—regardless of the particularities of the case at hand [@healy2017].
The third step is therefore to compile an appropriate overview of analytic results in summary form (whether statistical or otherwise).

In Lind’s example, the fitted ERGM supplies this summary, including both model-specification details and corresponding results for the network features it identifies as important.^[These should include *all* details necessary to estimate *and* interpret the model. In the case of ERGM, these are returned as part of the model object and include such information as model coefficients and standard errors, goodness-of-fit statistics, and convergence diagnostics [@krivitsky2023].]
The results elements of the *Grey's* example include gender *heter*ophily and a restriction on isolates.^[This excludes also investigated examples of age or racial homophily. Since formal goodness-of-fit statistics indicated including these produced more poorly performing models, they are excluded from the final results.]

### Step 4: Generate a modeled network from that summary

The fourth step is then to convert that summary into a “predicted” network that conforms to the key features of the estimated analytic results.
This modeled network visualization will necessarily differ from any observed network visualization by eliminating features that are not “modeled” [@schwabish2021], reducing the prominence of idiosyncratic variation (i.e., identifying “what is this a case of?” [@ragin1992; @collins2024]), and highlighting only the key elements of the findings that warrant theoretical interpretation [@vertesi2025].
The idea here is to provide an empirically anchored, theoretically prioritized, network visualization that clearly communicates the researchers’ key interpretative takeaways.

In [**Figure 2**](#fig:greys), panel B visualizes a single draw from the ERGM results for the *Grey’s Anatomy* analysis, allowing comparison with the observed network in panel A.
The modeled visualization includes only the aspects incorporated in the model, while diminishing the role of idiosyncratic aspects of the data.^[Here, the visual specifically excludes node labels and nodal attributes of race and age because goodness-of-fit statistics confirmed that these did not contribute to the observed relational pattern. More formal goodness-of-fit tests also confirm the “visual” similarity between the general structures of the two graphs, while other, lesser-performing models showed obvious divergences, visually *and* statistically.]

Not including names does not diminish the ability to observe important features of the network (e.g., a general, but not absolute, heterosexual partnering pattern).
More fundamentally, observed data provide only a single, characterization of reality, invariably including error along with the information they convey.^[Treating the realized particulars of that instance as central can over-reify what is often only an approximation--though ideally a reasonable one--of the theoretical question being investigated [@becker2017].]
As such using unlabeled nodes,^[Here we have not merely “removed” labels, but by presenting a modeled network, the nodes are not one-to-one mappings to real data points in any meaningful sense.] helps draw our attention to the interpretive implications of our analysis rather than toward the idiosyncrasies of the case at hand [@becker2017].
Furthermore, if these were actual data carrying confidentiality concerns, the modeled visualization—and its rendering of modeled results as unlabeled, “representative” nodes and ties rather than a capture of actual relationships—would also remove risks of sequential deductive disclosure.^[For example, given the infrequency of same-sex or inter-racial relationships in the population, even an *unlabeled* version of the graph on the left would allow partners of Derek or “Chief” to likely identify *themselves* in the plot, and thus “discover” their partners having other partners.]
Moreover, because the visual is based on model results, the model-results object is likely shareable even if the raw data are not,^[It is not uncommon in social network projects to have data-sharing restrictions as part of participation agreements as a means to ensure confidentiality.] facilitating the replicability of both the results and the visualization.

## Quo Vadimus?

\textcolor{red}{This is merely a sketch and a collection point for potential stray ideas to revisit, not at all a draft section yet.}

As with any visualization strategy, useful examples in the literature are joined by many that are, well, not so much.
There are numerous routes to less-informative (network) visualizations that can be avoided by following basic guidelines of visualization--e.g., unintelligible "hairball," poor layout choices, over-complicate visuals, and other visualization "sins" arise from poor implementation per se [@tufte1983].
However, a similar weakness arise if we assume visualization is a single task with "global optimization" principles. 
Developing a single visualization strategy intended to simultaneously serve multiple (potentially completing) purposes, *and* adhering to principles of sound research, can overly compromise the utility of the visuals we construct.

Despite these potential pitfall, network visualizations have undoubtedly proven to be an incredibly powerful part of our research toolkit. 
In this paper I've sought to think of visualization as more than a hammer in that bag, encouraging us instead to think of it as representing multiple options in that toolkit, each with different optimal uses.
Model-based visualization adds to those already available, providing an approach that is especially attuned to conveying theoretical implications of modeled empirical results
